# Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision

**Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Tao Xu, Greg Brockman, Christine McLeavey, Ilya Sutskever**  
*OpenAI, San Francisco, CA*  
*arXiv:2212.04356 (December 2022)*

---

## Abstract

A central problem in automatic speech recognition (ASR) is that models optimized on a
single data distribution achieve low error rates on that distribution but fail to generalize,
making far more errors than humans when applied to different acoustic environments, speakers,
or recording conditions. We study whether this robustness gap can be closed by a different
training recipe: scaling weakly supervised pretraining — using noisily labeled internet
audio — to 680,000 hours across 96 languages and four speech processing tasks. The
resulting model family, Whisper, uses an encoder-decoder Transformer trained entirely by
predicting transcript tokens from audio-transcript pairs collected from the internet. Without
any dataset-specific fine-tuning, zero-shot Whisper achieves 55.2% average relative error
reduction over a comparably performing supervised model when evaluated on 13 out-of-distribution
speech benchmarks. The best Whisper model approaches human-level accuracy and robustness
on English speech, reaches competitive or better zero-shot performance on speech-to-English
translation and multilingual recognition, and outperforms commercial ASR services on most
long-form transcription benchmarks. Performance is limited on low-resource languages and
language identification, and fine-tuning was not studied. Models and inference code are
publicly released.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 The In-Distribution Trap

In 2015, Deep Speech 2 (Amodei et al., 2015) reported a speech recognition system matching
human-level performance on the LibriSpeech benchmark — clean audiobook recordings — and
suggested there was little room for improvement without further domain adaptation. Seven
years later, the state-of-the-art word error rate (WER) on that benchmark had fallen another
73%, from 5.3% to 1.4% (Zhang et al., 2021), far below the reported human error rate of
5.8%. These improvements are remarkable. Yet they do not translate: models trained on
LibriSpeech remain far above human error rates when applied to conversational telephone
speech, noisy crowd environments, recordings of African American Vernacular English, or
earnings call audio.

*Word error rate* (WER) is the standard evaluation metric in ASR, measuring the proportion
of words that must be substituted, deleted, or inserted to match a reference transcript.
A model that achieves "superhuman" WER on a single benchmark may still commit basic errors
that a human would never make, because it has learned dataset-specific patterns — formatting
conventions, speaker name templates, silence distributions — that reliably predict reference
transcript tokens on held-out data from the *same* source without reflecting genuine
robustness to varied speech. This phenomenon, "shortcut learning" (Geirhos et al., 2020),
is the central problem motivating this work.

### 1.2 Why Current Approaches Fall Short

The dominant paradigm for high-performance ASR combines unsupervised or self-supervised
audio pretraining with dataset-specific supervised fine-tuning. Models such as wav2vec 2.0
(Baevski et al., 2020) learn audio representations from up to 1,000,000 hours of unlabeled
speech (Zhang et al., 2021), but these representations do not produce usable transcripts
on their own — a supervised decoder must be fine-tuned for each deployment distribution.
This fine-tuning step reintroduces distributional specificity, training the decoder to
exploit the exact formatting conventions and vocabulary distributions of the target evaluation
dataset.

An alternative approach trains supervised models across multiple datasets simultaneously,
improving robustness through distributional breadth (Narayanan et al., 2018; Likhomanenko
et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2021). The largest such effort, SpeechStew (Chan et al., 2021),
combines seven datasets totalling 5,140 hours — meaningful in scope but small by modern
data standards, and limited by the amount of high-quality labeled audio that exists.

In computer vision, an analogous challenge was addressed by scaling weakly supervised
pretraining far beyond available high-quality labeled data: training on billions of noisily
labeled internet images substantially improved model robustness and zero-shot generalization
(Mahajan et al., 2018; Kolesnikov et al., 2020; Radford et al., 2021). This paper asks
whether the same strategy works for speech.

### 1.3 This Work

This paper presents Whisper, a speech recognition system trained on 680,000 hours of
audio paired with transcripts collected from the internet. This is approximately two orders
of magnitude more labeled data than prior multi-domain supervised speech approaches and an
order of magnitude more than prior weakly supervised efforts (Chen et al., 2021; Galvez et
al., 2021). Whisper is trained entirely with supervised next-token prediction objectives —
no self-supervised or self-training auxiliary losses are used.

Beyond scale, Whisper handles multiple speech processing tasks within a single model:
multilingual transcription in 96 languages, speech-to-English translation, voice activity
detection, and spoken language identification. All tasks are specified through special tokens
prepended to the decoder input, requiring no architectural changes across tasks. We evaluate
Whisper entirely in a zero-shot setting — no training data from any evaluation benchmark is
used — across 25+ academic datasets spanning diverse acoustic conditions, languages, and
tasks.

---

## 2. Background

### 2.1 Automatic Speech Recognition and Word Error Rate

Automatic speech recognition converts spoken audio into a written transcript. The standard
metric, word error rate, measures string edit distance normalized by reference length:

> WER = (Substitutions + Deletions + Insertions) / Reference words × 100%

WER is sensitive to transcript formatting: whether numbers are spelled out, whether
contractions are expanded, whether punctuation is present. A model that writes
"sixty-eight million dollars" where a reference writes "$68 million" incurs word errors
despite conveying identical information. This creates an evaluation challenge for models
not fine-tuned on a specific dataset's formatting conventions — a particular concern for
zero-shot evaluation. The authors address this through text normalization before WER
calculation, standardizing formatting differences that do not reflect genuine transcription
errors.

### 2.2 The Robustness Gap in ASR

Taori et al. (2020) formalized *effective robustness* for image classifiers: how a model
performs on out-of-distribution data *relative to* what its in-distribution performance
would predict. A model with high effective robustness performs as well as expected under
distribution shift; one with low effective robustness degrades faster than expected. The
same concept applies to ASR: given a model's WER on LibriSpeech — the community's standard
reference benchmark — how does it perform on other evaluation sets? As this paper
demonstrates, supervised LibriSpeech models have low effective robustness, performing
roughly twice as badly as humans on diverse real-world benchmarks despite matching human
WER on LibriSpeech.

### 2.3 Weak Supervision via Internet Data

"Weak supervision" in this context means using transcripts collected from the internet —
closed captions, user-contributed subtitles, automatically generated captions — rather
than transcripts produced under controlled quality conditions by paid annotators. Such data
is abundant but noisy: some transcripts are generated by other ASR systems, misaligned with
audio, or in the wrong language. The working hypothesis, supported by results in computer
vision, is that the diversity and scale of internet data outweigh its lower per-example
quality for learning representations that generalize robustly.

---

## 3. Method

### 3.1 Training Data

The Whisper training dataset contains 680,000 hours of audio paired with transcripts
collected from the internet, spanning many recording environments, speaking styles, languages,
and acoustic conditions. Of the total, 438,218 hours cover English speech recognition,
117,113 hours cover multilingual speech recognition in 96 non-English languages, and
125,739 hours cover audio-to-English speech translation.

Internet-sourced transcripts vary widely in quality. Many are generated by other ASR
systems rather than human transcribers; training on such data can impair model quality
(Ghorbani et al., 2021). The authors developed several filtering steps: heuristics to
detect and discard machine-generated transcripts (exploiting signals such as absence of
complex punctuation and all-uppercase or all-lowercase formatting), audio language
detection to ensure transcript and audio languages match, and fuzzy deduplication of
transcripts. A prototype Whisper model was used in a second filtering pass to identify
high-error training sources for manual inspection. Overlap with key evaluation datasets
was removed. Audio was segmented into 30-second chunks resampled to 16,000 Hz.

### 3.2 Model Architecture

Whisper uses an encoder-decoder Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), the same architecture
class widely used for sequence-to-sequence tasks in natural language processing. Five
model sizes were trained:

| Size   | Parameters | Layers | Width | Attention Heads |
|--------|-----------|--------|-------|-----------------|
| Tiny   | 39 M      | 4      | 384   | 6               |
| Base   | 74 M      | 6      | 512   | 8               |
| Small  | 244 M     | 12     | 768   | 12              |
| Medium | 769 M     | 24     | 1,024 | 16              |
| Large  | 1,550 M   | 32     | 1,280 | 20              |

The audio encoder takes as input an 80-channel log-magnitude Mel spectrogram — a
time-frequency representation of the audio waveform computed on 25 ms windows at a
10 ms stride. Two convolutional layers compress the spectrogram before Transformer
encoder blocks with sinusoidal position embeddings process it. The decoder uses learned
position embeddings and ties its input and output token embeddings. The byte-level BPE
tokenizer from GPT-2 (Sennrich et al., 2015; Radford et al., 2019) is used for
English-only models; the vocabulary is refitted for multilingual models to avoid
fragmentation of non-English scripts.

### 3.3 Multitask Training Format

A defining design choice is that all four speech processing tasks are expressed as
next-token prediction over a shared vocabulary, conditioned on special tokens that
specify the task. Before generating the transcript, the decoder is conditioned on:

1. `<|startoftranscript|>` — beginning-of-output marker
2. A *language token* (one of 99 tags identifying the spoken language, sourced from a
   language detection model)
3. A *task token* — `<|transcribe|>` for ASR or `<|translate|>` for speech-to-English
   translation
4. A *timestamp token* — `<|notimestamps|>` for text-only output, or a beginning timestamp
   for time-aligned transcription
5. A `<|nospeech|>` token — when the audio segment contains no speech

This format means voice activity detection, language identification, transcription, and
translation all share the same forward pass and the same learned parameters, differing only
in the conditioning tokens. With some probability during training, the transcript of the
preceding audio segment is prepended to the decoder input, encouraging the model to use
long-range text context.

### 3.4 Training Details

Models were trained with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) and gradient norm clipping
(Pascanu et al., 2013), with a linear learning rate decay to zero after 2,048 warmup steps,
a batch size of 256 audio segments, and 2^20 total update steps (two to three passes over
the dataset). Because so few epochs are used on such a large dataset, overfitting was not
a concern; no data augmentation or regularization was applied in the base training runs.
All models were trained in mixed precision (FP16) with data parallelism.

An improved variant — Large V2, the best model in all reported comparisons — was trained
for 2.5 times more update steps with three regularization techniques added: SpecAugment
(Park et al., 2019), Stochastic Depth (Huang et al., 2016), and BPE Dropout (Provilkov
et al., 2019). All Large model results below refer to Large V2 unless otherwise noted.

---

## 4. Results

All evaluations are performed in a *zero-shot* setting: no training data from any evaluation
benchmark is used. Text normalization is applied before WER computation to reduce
penalization of formatting differences that do not reflect genuine transcription errors.

### 4.1 English Speech Recognition: Robustness Across Distributions

The central experimental question is whether zero-shot Whisper generalizes better across
distributions than supervised models trained on a single curated dataset. LibriSpeech is
used as the reference distribution because many publicly released supervised models train
on it, enabling a controlled robustness comparison: two models matched on LibriSpeech WER
are compared on 13 other benchmarks.

The comparison pair is wav2vec 2.0 Large (no language model), a strong supervised baseline,
and zero-shot Whisper Large V2. Both achieve 2.7% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean —
in-distribution performance is effectively identical. The 13 out-of-distribution benchmarks
span spontaneous conversational speech (Switchboard, CallHome), noisy multi-speaker
recordings (CHiME-6, AMI), diverse online speech (Common Voice, Artie bias corpus),
regional dialect recordings (CORAAL), broadcasted read speech (WSJ), political speech
(VoxPopuli), TED talks (TED-LIUM), and general English audio (Fleurs).

| Dataset              | wav2vec 2.0 Large (WER%) | Whisper Large V2 (WER%) | Rel. Error Reduction |
|----------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------|----------------------|
| LibriSpeech clean    | 2.7                      | 2.7                     | 0% (reference)       |
| Artie                | 24.5                     | 6.2                     | 74.7%                |
| Common Voice         | 29.9                     | 9.0                     | 69.9%                |
| Fleurs En            | 14.6                     | 4.4                     | 69.9%                |
| TED-LIUM             | 10.5                     | 4.0                     | 61.9%                |
| CHiME-6              | 65.8                     | 25.5                    | 61.2%                |
| VoxPopuli En         | 17.9                     | 7.3                     | 59.2%                |
| CORAAL               | 35.6                     | 16.2                    | 54.5%                |
| AMI (IHM)            | 37.0                     | 16.9                    | 54.3%                |
| Switchboard          | 28.3                     | 13.8                    | 51.2%                |
| CallHome             | 34.8                     | 17.6                    | 49.4%                |
| WSJ                  | 7.7                      | 3.9                     | 49.4%                |
| AMI (SDM1)           | 67.6                     | 36.4                    | 46.2%                |
| LibriSpeech other    | 6.2                      | 5.2                     | 16.1%                |
| **Average (13 OOD)** | **29.3**                 | **12.8**                | **55.2%**            |

*Table 1: Effective robustness comparison. Both models achieve 2.7% WER on LibriSpeech
test-clean; on 13 other datasets, zero-shot Whisper achieves 55.2% average relative error
reduction. Results after text normalization. Relative error reduction computed as
(baseline WER − Whisper WER) / baseline WER. (Source: Table 2 in Radford et al., 2022.)*

The 55.2% average relative error reduction holds while in-distribution performance is
controlled. The benefit does not require the largest model: a 39-million-parameter Whisper
Tiny with 6.7% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean is "roughly competitive with the best
supervised LibriSpeech model when evaluated on other datasets," as the authors describe.
The robustness advantage thus appears to be a property of training data diversity rather
than model scale specifically.

### 4.2 Comparison with Human Performance

To assess where Whisper sits relative to human transcribers, the authors computed a
*robustness frontier*: for each zero-shot Whisper model size, they plotted average WER on
three out-of-distribution datasets against WER on LibriSpeech. Supervised LibriSpeech
models cluster far above this frontier — they are less robust than expected given their
in-distribution performance. The estimated robustness frontier of zero-shot Whisper models
includes the 95% confidence interval for a single human evaluator's performance on those
same datasets.

A more direct comparison was conducted on 25 recordings from the Kincaid46 dataset,
a collection of diverse audio including scripted broadcast, unscripted interviews, telephone
calls, and meetings. Five professional transcription services provided reference transcripts:
four entirely human, one computer-assisted. The computer-assisted service achieved the
lowest aggregate WER, 1.15 percentage points lower than Whisper. The four purely human
transcription services performed only a fraction of a percentage point better than Whisper
on the same 25 recordings. The authors note that Whisper's English ASR performance is "not
perfect but very close to human-level accuracy."

### 4.3 Multilingual Speech Recognition

On Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS, Pratap et al., 2020b), which covers 8 European languages,
zero-shot Whisper achieves 7.3% WER, outperforming fine-tuned XLS-R (Babu et al., 2021)
at 10.9% and matching Maestro (Chen et al., 2022b) at 7.3%. On VoxPopuli (Wang et al.,
2021), covering 16 European languages, Whisper (13.6% WER) lags substantially behind
Maestro (8.1%), which the authors attribute to other models using VoxPopuli as a major
unsupervised pretraining source and to VoxPopuli having roughly 10× more supervised data
per language than MLS.

Performance across a broader language set was studied on the Fleurs dataset (Conneau et
al., 2022), covering 102 languages. A strong log-log linear relationship exists between
the amount of per-language training data and zero-shot WER (r² = 0.83), with WER
approximately halving for every 16-fold increase in training hours. Languages that deviate
from this trend — performing worse than predicted — tend to have unique scripts or are
linguistically distant from the Indo-European majority of the training set (Hebrew, Telugu,
Chinese, Korean). The training dataset is English-heavy due to internet data collection
biases, and most non-English languages have fewer than 1,000 hours of training data;
performance on low-resource languages remains correspondingly poor.

### 4.4 Speech-to-English Translation

On CoVoST 2 (Wang et al., 2020b), which covers translation from 21 source languages to
English, zero-shot Whisper achieves 29.1 BLEU overall, improving over mSLAM-CTC (24.8)
and Maestro (25.2). The advantage is most pronounced on low-resource languages: on the
lowest-resource group, Whisper achieves 25.2 BLEU versus mSLAM's 18.5, a gain of 6.7
BLEU attributable to the far larger translation training data in Whisper's pretraining set
(68,000 hours for these languages versus 861 total hours in CoVoST2's training split). On
high-resource languages, Whisper (36.2 BLEU) does not match Maestro (38.2) or mSLAM (37.8).
The authors caution that the text standardizer used in this evaluation was developed
alongside Whisper, which precludes confident state-of-the-art claims.

### 4.5 Language Identification

Zero-shot Whisper achieves 64.5% language identification accuracy on the Fleurs benchmark,
substantially below the supervised state of the art (mSLAM-CTC: 77.7%). However, this
comparison is confounded: Whisper has no training data for 20 of the 102 Fleurs languages,
placing a structural ceiling on its accuracy at 80.4%. On the 82 languages where Whisper
does have training data, it achieves 80.3% — within 0.1 percentage points of the ceiling.
Language identification performance is therefore primarily constrained by training data
coverage rather than representational capacity.

### 4.6 Long-form Transcription

Whisper's 30-second context window requires a sliding-window strategy for audio longer than
30 seconds: the window shifts according to the timestamps predicted by the model. The authors
developed decoding heuristics to reduce failure modes (repetition loops, hallucination):
5-beam search, temperature fallback when outputs are implausibly repetitive or have low
log-probability, voice activity detection to skip silent segments, and previous-text
conditioning for cross-window context continuity. Applied incrementally, these reduce average
WER across seven long-form datasets from 11.0% (greedy decoding only) to 10.0% (full
heuristic stack).

On those seven benchmarks — TED talks, podcasts, late-night television, earnings calls, and
recorded interviews — Whisper outperforms all compared open-source ASR models and performs
better than four commercial ASR services on most benchmarks. The authors note that some
commercial services may have been trained on portions of these publicly available datasets,
making the comparison approximate.

---

## 5. Analysis and Ablations

### 5.1 Model Scale

Performance improves with model size across multilingual speech recognition, translation,
and language identification for all five model sizes from 39 M to 1,550 M parameters. English
speech recognition shows diminishing returns at larger model sizes, consistent with the
hypothesis that English ASR is approaching a human-level performance ceiling where model
capacity is no longer the bottleneck.

### 5.2 Dataset Scale

A medium-sized model was trained on subsets ranging from 0.5% to 100% of the 680,000-hour
dataset to measure data scaling effects:

| Training Hours | English WER (↓) | Multilingual WER (↓) | X→En BLEU (↑) |
|---------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------|
| 3,405         | 30.5            | 92.4                | 0.2           |
| 6,811         | 19.6            | 72.7                | 1.7           |
| 13,621        | 14.4            | 56.6                | 7.9           |
| 27,243        | 12.3            | 45.0                | 13.9          |
| 54,486        | 10.9            | 36.4                | 19.2          |
| 681,070       | 9.9             | 29.2                | 24.8          |

*Table 2: All metrics improve monotonically with training data size. English WER is an
average over 12 evaluation datasets; multilingual WER covers overlapping Fleurs languages;
X→En BLEU is averaged over CoVoST2. (Source: Table 6 in Radford et al., 2022.)*

All three tasks improve monotonically across all data scales. Translation BLEU is near zero
at or below 7,000 hours — a minimum-data threshold for this task to become functional at all
— then follows a roughly log-linear trend. Multilingual WER follows a power-law improvement
through 54,000 hours. English WER improves rapidly from 3,000 to 13,000 hours then slows,
again consistent with approaching a saturation regime. At the largest scale (54,000 to
681,070 hours), all tasks show diminishing returns, which the authors interpret as either
under-training relative to dataset size or a genuine plateau in data-scaling benefits for
speech recognition.

### 5.3 Multitask and Multilingual Transfer

A natural concern with joint multitask training is *negative transfer*: interference between
tasks degrading performance on each individual task compared to a task-specific model. The
authors tested this by comparing English-only models with jointly trained models at equal
compute, adjusting for the fraction of compute devoted to English SR (65% in joint training).

At small model sizes, joint training does hurt English SR — negative transfer is real and
measurable. However, as model size and compute increase, joint models improve faster and
eventually surpass English-only models. At the largest experiments, joint training yields
slightly better English SR even without any compute adjustment. This pattern suggests that
exposure to diverse multilingual speech improves acoustic representations in ways that
benefit English SR, but only when the model is large enough to learn both without conflict.

### 5.4 Noise Robustness

Whisper was compared against 14 ASR models from the literature under additive white noise
and pub noise (ambient restaurant sound) across a range of signal-to-noise ratios (SNR).
Under low noise (40 dB SNR), many models outperform Whisper — expected, as those models
train primarily on clean LibriSpeech-style audio. Under high noise (SNR below 10 dB),
all 14 compared models perform worse than Whisper under pub noise. Whisper's robustness
advantage is thus most pronounced under the naturalistic distribution shifts that correspond
to real-world noisy environments.

### 5.5 Text Normalization Validity

The text normalizer used for WER computation was developed alongside Whisper, raising the
concern that it might discount formatting errors that Whisper specifically makes more often
than other models. Comparing against the independently developed FairSpeech normalizer
(Koenecke et al., 2020), the two normalizers produce similar relative WER differences on
most benchmarks. On three benchmarks — WSJ, CallHome, and Switchboard — the authors'
normalizer benefits Whisper noticeably more than it benefits comparison models, due to
specific formatting conventions (number expressions, common contractions) handled more
permissively. The authors acknowledge this evaluation bias on those specific benchmarks.

---

## 6. Discussion

### 6.1 Distributional Coverage as the Driver of Robustness

The central result — that a zero-shot model trained on diverse weakly labeled internet data
substantially outperforms a supervised model matched on an in-distribution benchmark —
points to a specific explanation for the ASR robustness gap: models trained on a single
dataset distribution learn dataset-specific patterns that generalize within that distribution
but not beyond it. This is a manifestation of "shortcut learning" (Geirhos et al., 2020):
the model solves the right task on the training distribution but learns the wrong
representation. Whisper's training distribution — 680,000 hours of internet audio spanning
thousands of environments, domains, languages, and recording conditions — acts as a
regularizer against any single such shortcut. The 55.2% average relative error reduction
over the supervised baseline measures how much benefit that distributional breadth provides
compared to in-distribution specialization.

### 6.2 Reframing the Comparison with Human Performance

A recurring claim in ASR research is that models have achieved "superhuman" performance on
LibriSpeech. The paper's authors argue that this comparison is misleading. The difference
between machine and human performance on a benchmark arises not from the test but from the
training: humans transcribing a benchmark audio sample have never been trained on
LibriSpeech-style audio, so they are tested for out-of-distribution generalization. A machine
model trained on LibriSpeech is tested for in-distribution generalization. Both are
evaluated on the same test data, but two different abilities are being measured.

This framing explains why zero-shot Whisper, not supervised LibriSpeech models, approaches
human robustness across benchmarks (Figure 2 in the paper): its training regime more closely
mirrors how humans develop speech competence — broad exposure to varied speech rather than
intensive practice on a specific narrow distribution.

### 6.3 Connection to Weak Supervision at Scale in Vision

Whisper's success is directly analogous to results from large-scale weak supervision in
computer vision. Models trained on internet images with noisy labels (Mahajan et al., 2018)
or on image-text pairs from the web (Radford et al., 2021; Kolesnikov et al., 2020) showed
dramatically improved robustness and zero-shot transfer. In both cases, the enabling factor
appears to be that internet-scale diversity forces the model to learn representations close
to the semantic content of the data, rather than dataset-specific surface features. Whisper
provides evidence that this principle extends from images to audio.

### 6.4 Limitations

**Fine-tuning not evaluated.** The entire study focuses on zero-shot transfer. For practical
deployments where labeled in-domain data is available, fine-tuning Whisper could improve
performance substantially beyond the zero-shot numbers reported here; this remains unstudied.

**Low-resource language performance.** The training dataset is English-heavy due to
internet data collection biases. Most non-English languages have fewer than 1,000 hours of
training data, and performance on low-resource languages remains poor. The strong scaling
law (r² = 0.83) makes clear that performance would improve with targeted data collection for
these languages, but this has not been done.

**Long-form decoding failures.** Hallucination, repetition loops, and failure to transcribe
the first or last few words of a segment are known failure modes of the sequence-to-sequence
generation approach used in long-form transcription. The heuristic decoding strategy
described in Section 4.6 substantially reduces these failures but does not eliminate them.

**Evaluation fairness.** The text normalizer was co-developed with Whisper, introducing
modest bias on some benchmarks (notably WSJ, CallHome, Switchboard). The comparison with
commercial ASR services is imperfect because those services may have trained on the
evaluation datasets. The human comparison uses only 25 recordings without reported confidence
intervals.

**Language identification.** While Whisper achieves 80.3% on languages it was trained on,
the overall Fleurs accuracy (64.5%) is substantially below the supervised state of the art
(77.7%), primarily because of the 20 languages for which Whisper has no training data.

---

## 7. Related Work

### 7.1 Scaling in Automatic Speech Recognition

Scale — of models, data, and compute — has consistently improved ASR performance over the
past decade. Deep Speech 2 (Amodei et al., 2015) scaled to 12,000 hours with distributed
GPU training. Narayanan et al. (2018) used semi-supervised pretraining to reach 162,000
hours of labeled audio. BigSSL (Zhang et al., 2021) pushed unsupervised pretraining to
1,000,000 hours with multi-billion-parameter fine-tuned models. Earlier weakly supervised
efforts (Chen et al., 2021; Galvez et al., 2021) scaled labeled speech to 10,000–30,000
hours. Whisper occupies a distinct point in this space: 680,000 hours of supervised
(though noisily labeled) pretraining without an unsupervised pretraining stage.

### 7.2 Self-supervised Speech Pretraining

wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020) demonstrated that self-supervised contrastive learning
on unlabeled audio could learn representations that, when fine-tuned with a supervised
decoder, compete with fully supervised baselines. HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021a) improved this
with masked prediction of pseudo-labels. XLS-R (Babu et al., 2021) scaled multilingual
self-supervised pretraining. These models share an important property that Whisper's
approach avoids: the pretrained encoder alone cannot produce transcripts; a separate
supervised decoder must be learned for each deployment distribution.

### 7.3 Multitask and Multilingual Learning for Speech

Multitask learning for speech has a long history. Toshniwal et al. (2018) jointly trained
a single model across multiple languages. Pratap et al. (2020a) scaled this to 50 languages
with a billion-parameter model. mSLAM (Bapna et al., 2022) extended joint pretraining to
cover both speech and text. Whisper's specific contribution is using a token-based
conditioning format to cover four heterogeneous speech processing tasks within a single
decoder without architectural changes, and demonstrating that at sufficient scale this
training is mutually beneficial across all tasks.

### 7.4 Robustness to Distribution Shift

The robustness of machine learning models to distribution shift has been studied across
image classification (Taori et al., 2020), natural language processing (Hendrycks et al.,
2020), and question answering (Miller et al., 2020). A consistent finding is that multi-domain
training improves robustness — a finding that Whisper confirms for speech at an
unprecedented scale. The connection to CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) is direct: both works
demonstrate that sufficiently large and diverse weakly supervised training can produce
zero-shot performance that matches task-specific supervised models on reference benchmarks
while far exceeding them on out-of-distribution evaluations.

---

## 8. Conclusion

Whisper demonstrates that the robustness gap between human and machine speech recognition
is not primarily a model capacity problem but a training distribution problem. A single
encoder-decoder Transformer trained on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised internet audio —
without self-supervised pretraining, without dataset-specific fine-tuning, and without data
augmentation — achieves 55.2% average relative error reduction over a comparable supervised
model on 13 diverse out-of-distribution benchmarks, approaches human accuracy on English
speech, reaches zero-shot performance competitive with or better than prior work on speech
translation and multilingual recognition, and outperforms commercial ASR systems on most
long-form transcription benchmarks.

The central lesson is that scaling weakly supervised pretraining with diverse internet data
has been underappreciated in speech recognition research relative to the dominant unsupervised
pretraining paradigm. Diverse supervised data at sufficient scale appears to produce the
same generalizable acoustic and linguistic representations that human listeners develop
through broad exposure to varied speech — and that breadth, not in-distribution
specialization, produces robust human-like performance.

Key open problems include improving performance on low-resource languages through targeted
data collection, addressing long-form transcription failure modes through better decoding
strategies, and studying the benefits of fine-tuning on specific deployment distributions.

---

# Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision

**Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Tao Xu, Greg Brockman, Christine McLeavey, Ilya Sutskever**  
*OpenAI, San Francisco, CA*  
*arXiv:2212.04356 (December 2022)*

---

## Abstract

A central problem in automatic speech recognition (ASR) is that models optimized on a
single data distribution achieve low error rates on that distribution but fail to generalize,
making far more errors than humans when applied to different acoustic environments, speakers,
or recording conditions. We study whether this robustness gap can be closed by a different
training recipe: scaling weakly supervised pretraining — using noisily labeled internet
audio — to 680,000 hours across 96 languages and four speech processing tasks. The
resulting model family, Whisper, uses an encoder-decoder Transformer trained entirely by
predicting transcript tokens from audio-transcript pairs collected from the internet. Without
any dataset-specific fine-tuning, zero-shot Whisper achieves 55.2% average relative error
reduction over a comparably performing supervised model when evaluated on 13 out-of-distribution
speech benchmarks. The best Whisper model approaches human-level accuracy and robustness
on English speech, reaches competitive or better zero-shot performance on speech-to-English
translation and multilingual recognition, and outperforms commercial ASR services on most
long-form transcription benchmarks. Performance is limited on low-resource languages and
language identification, and fine-tuning was not studied. Models and inference code are
publicly released.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 The In-Distribution Trap

In 2015, Deep Speech 2 (Amodei et al., 2015) reported a speech recognition system matching
human-level performance on the LibriSpeech benchmark — clean audiobook recordings — and
suggested there was little room for improvement without further domain adaptation. Seven
years later, the state-of-the-art word error rate (WER) on that benchmark had fallen another
73%, from 5.3% to 1.4% (Zhang et al., 2021), far below the reported human error rate of
5.8%. These improvements are remarkable. Yet they do not translate: models trained on
LibriSpeech remain far above human error rates when applied to conversational telephone
speech, noisy crowd environments, recordings of African American Vernacular English, or
earnings call audio.

*Word error rate* (WER) is the standard evaluation metric in ASR, measuring the proportion
of words that must be substituted, deleted, or inserted to match a reference transcript.
A model that achieves "superhuman" WER on a single benchmark may still commit basic errors
that a human would never make, because it has learned dataset-specific patterns — formatting
conventions, speaker name templates, silence distributions — that reliably predict reference
transcript tokens on held-out data from the *same* source without reflecting genuine
robustness to varied speech. This phenomenon, "shortcut learning" (Geirhos et al., 2020),
is the central problem motivating this work.

### 1.2 Why Current Approaches Fall Short

The dominant paradigm for high-performance ASR combines unsupervised or self-supervised
audio pretraining with dataset-specific supervised fine-tuning. Models such as wav2vec 2.0
(Baevski et al., 2020) learn audio representations from up to 1,000,000 hours of unlabeled
speech (Zhang et al., 2021), but these representations do not produce usable transcripts
on their own — a supervised decoder must be fine-tuned for each deployment distribution.
This fine-tuning step reintroduces distributional specificity, training the decoder to
exploit the exact formatting conventions and vocabulary distributions of the target evaluation
dataset.

An alternative approach trains supervised models across multiple datasets simultaneously,
improving robustness through distributional breadth (Narayanan et al., 2018; Likhomanenko
et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2021). The largest such effort, SpeechStew (Chan et al., 2021),
combines seven datasets totalling 5,140 hours — meaningful in scope but small by modern
data standards, and limited by the amount of high-quality labeled audio that exists.

In computer vision, an analogous challenge was addressed by scaling weakly supervised
pretraining far beyond available high-quality labeled data: training on billions of noisily
labeled internet images substantially improved model robustness and zero-shot generalization
(Mahajan et al., 2018; Kolesnikov et al., 2020; Radford et al., 2021). This paper asks
whether the same strategy works for speech.

### 1.3 This Work

This paper presents Whisper, a speech recognition system trained on 680,000 hours of
audio paired with transcripts collected from the internet. This is approximately two orders
of magnitude more labeled data than prior multi-domain supervised speech approaches and an
order of magnitude more than prior weakly supervised efforts (Chen et al., 2021; Galvez et
al., 2021). Whisper is trained entirely with supervised next-token prediction objectives —
no self-supervised or self-training auxiliary losses are used.

Beyond scale, Whisper handles multiple speech processing tasks within a single model:
multilingual transcription in 96 languages, speech-to-English translation, voice activity
detection, and spoken language identification. All tasks are specified through special tokens
prepended to the decoder input, requiring no architectural changes across tasks. We evaluate
Whisper entirely in a zero-shot setting — no training data from any evaluation benchmark is
used — across 25+ academic datasets spanning diverse acoustic conditions, languages, and
tasks.

---

## 2. Background

### 2.1 Automatic Speech Recognition and Word Error Rate

Automatic speech recognition converts spoken audio into a written transcript. The standard
metric, word error rate, measures string edit distance normalized by reference length:

> WER = (Substitutions + Deletions + Insertions) / Reference words × 100%

WER is sensitive to transcript formatting: whether numbers are spelled out, whether
contractions are expanded, whether punctuation is present. A model that writes
"sixty-eight million dollars" where a reference writes "$68 million" incurs word errors
despite conveying identical information. This creates an evaluation challenge for models
not fine-tuned on a specific dataset's formatting conventions — a particular concern for
zero-shot evaluation. The authors address this through text normalization before WER
calculation, standardizing formatting differences that do not reflect genuine transcription
errors.

### 2.2 The Robustness Gap in ASR

Taori et al. (2020) formalized *effective robustness* for image classifiers: how a model
performs on out-of-distribution data *relative to* what its in-distribution performance
would predict. A model with high effective robustness performs as well as expected under
distribution shift; one with low effective robustness degrades faster than expected. The
same concept applies to ASR: given a model's WER on LibriSpeech — the community's standard
reference benchmark — how does it perform on other evaluation sets? As this paper
demonstrates, supervised LibriSpeech models have low effective robustness, performing
roughly twice as badly as humans on diverse real-world benchmarks despite matching human
WER on LibriSpeech.

### 2.3 Weak Supervision via Internet Data

"Weak supervision" in this context means using transcripts collected from the internet —
closed captions, user-contributed subtitles, automatically generated captions — rather
than transcripts produced under controlled quality conditions by paid annotators. Such data
is abundant but noisy: some transcripts are generated by other ASR systems, misaligned with
audio, or in the wrong language. The working hypothesis, supported by results in computer
vision, is that the diversity and scale of internet data outweigh its lower per-example
quality for learning representations that generalize robustly.

---

## 3. Method

### 3.1 Training Data

The Whisper training dataset contains 680,000 hours of audio paired with transcripts
collected from the internet, spanning many recording environments, speaking styles, languages,
and acoustic conditions. Of the total, 438,218 hours cover English speech recognition,
117,113 hours cover multilingual speech recognition in 96 non-English languages, and
125,739 hours cover audio-to-English speech translation.

Internet-sourced transcripts vary widely in quality. Many are generated by other ASR
systems rather than human transcribers; training on such data can impair model quality
(Ghorbani et al., 2021). The authors developed several filtering steps: heuristics to
detect and discard machine-generated transcripts (exploiting signals such as absence of
complex punctuation and all-uppercase or all-lowercase formatting), audio language
detection to ensure transcript and audio languages match, and fuzzy deduplication of
transcripts. A prototype Whisper model was used in a second filtering pass to identify
high-error training sources for manual inspection. Overlap with key evaluation datasets
was removed. Audio was segmented into 30-second chunks resampled to 16,000 Hz.

### 3.2 Model Architecture

Whisper uses an encoder-decoder Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), the same architecture
class widely used for sequence-to-sequence tasks in natural language processing. Five
model sizes were trained:

| Size   | Parameters | Layers | Width | Attention Heads |
|--------|-----------|--------|-------|-----------------|
| Tiny   | 39 M      | 4      | 384   | 6               |
| Base   | 74 M      | 6      | 512   | 8               |
| Small  | 244 M     | 12     | 768   | 12              |
| Medium | 769 M     | 24     | 1,024 | 16              |
| Large  | 1,550 M   | 32     | 1,280 | 20              |

The audio encoder takes as input an 80-channel log-magnitude Mel spectrogram — a
time-frequency representation of the audio waveform computed on 25 ms windows at a
10 ms stride. Two convolutional layers compress the spectrogram before Transformer
encoder blocks with sinusoidal position embeddings process it. The decoder uses learned
position embeddings and ties its input and output token embeddings. The byte-level BPE
tokenizer from GPT-2 (Sennrich et al., 2015; Radford et al., 2019) is used for
English-only models; the vocabulary is refitted for multilingual models to avoid
fragmentation of non-English scripts.

### 3.3 Multitask Training Format

A defining design choice is that all four speech processing tasks are expressed as
next-token prediction over a shared vocabulary, conditioned on special tokens that
specify the task. Before generating the transcript, the decoder is conditioned on:

1. `<|startoftranscript|>` — beginning-of-output marker
2. A *language token* (one of 99 tags identifying the spoken language, sourced from a
   language detection model)
3. A *task token* — `<|transcribe|>` for ASR or `<|translate|>` for speech-to-English
   translation
4. A *timestamp token* — `<|notimestamps|>` for text-only output, or a beginning timestamp
   for time-aligned transcription
5. A `<|nospeech|>` token — when the audio segment contains no speech

This format means voice activity detection, language identification, transcription, and
translation all share the same forward pass and the same learned parameters, differing only
in the conditioning tokens. With some probability during training, the transcript of the
preceding audio segment is prepended to the decoder input, encouraging the model to use
long-range text context.

### 3.4 Training Details

Models were trained with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) and gradient norm clipping
(Pascanu et al., 2013), with a linear learning rate decay to zero after 2,048 warmup steps,
a batch size of 256 audio segments, and 2^20 total update steps (two to three passes over
the dataset). Because so few epochs are used on such a large dataset, overfitting was not
a concern; no data augmentation or regularization was applied in the base training runs.
All models were trained in mixed precision (FP16) with data parallelism.

An improved variant — Large V2, the best model in all reported comparisons — was trained
for 2.5 times more update steps with three regularization techniques added: SpecAugment
(Park et al., 2019), Stochastic Depth (Huang et al., 2016), and BPE Dropout (Provilkov
et al., 2019). All Large model results below refer to Large V2 unless otherwise noted.

---

## 4. Results

All evaluations are performed in a *zero-shot* setting: no training data from any evaluation
benchmark is used. Text normalization is applied before WER computation to reduce
penalization of formatting differences that do not reflect genuine transcription errors.

### 4.1 English Speech Recognition: Robustness Across Distributions

The central experimental question is whether zero-shot Whisper generalizes better across
distributions than supervised models trained on a single curated dataset. LibriSpeech is
used as the reference distribution because many publicly released supervised models train
on it, enabling a controlled robustness comparison: two models matched on LibriSpeech WER
are compared on 13 other benchmarks.

The comparison pair is wav2vec 2.0 Large (no language model), a strong supervised baseline,
and zero-shot Whisper Large V2. Both achieve 2.7% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean —
in-distribution performance is effectively identical. The 13 out-of-distribution benchmarks
span spontaneous conversational speech (Switchboard, CallHome), noisy multi-speaker
recordings (CHiME-6, AMI), diverse online speech (Common Voice, Artie bias corpus),
regional dialect recordings (CORAAL), broadcasted read speech (WSJ), political speech
(VoxPopuli), TED talks (TED-LIUM), and general English audio (Fleurs).

| Dataset              | wav2vec 2.0 Large (WER%) | Whisper Large V2 (WER%) | Rel. Error Reduction |
|----------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------|----------------------|
| LibriSpeech clean    | 2.7                      | 2.7                     | 0% (reference)       |
| Artie                | 24.5                     | 6.2                     | 74.7%                |
| Common Voice         | 29.9                     | 9.0                     | 69.9%                |
| Fleurs En            | 14.6                     | 4.4                     | 69.9%                |
| TED-LIUM             | 10.5                     | 4.0                     | 61.9%                |
| CHiME-6              | 65.8                     | 25.5                    | 61.2%                |
| VoxPopuli En         | 17.9                     | 7.3                     | 59.2%                |
| CORAAL               | 35.6                     | 16.2                    | 54.5%                |
| AMI (IHM)            | 37.0                     | 16.9                    | 54.3%                |
| Switchboard          | 28.3                     | 13.8                    | 51.2%                |
| CallHome             | 34.8                     | 17.6                    | 49.4%                |
| WSJ                  | 7.7                      | 3.9                     | 49.4%                |
| AMI (SDM1)           | 67.6                     | 36.4                    | 46.2%                |
| LibriSpeech other    | 6.2                      | 5.2                     | 16.1%                |
| **Average (13 OOD)** | **29.3**                 | **12.8**                | **55.2%**            |

*Table 1: Effective robustness comparison. Both models achieve 2.7% WER on LibriSpeech
test-clean; on 13 other datasets, zero-shot Whisper achieves 55.2% average relative error
reduction. Results after text normalization. Relative error reduction computed as
(baseline WER − Whisper WER) / baseline WER. (Source: Table 2 in Radford et al., 2022.)*

The 55.2% average relative error reduction holds while in-distribution performance is
controlled. The benefit does not require the largest model: a 39-million-parameter Whisper
Tiny with 6.7% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean is "roughly competitive with the best
supervised LibriSpeech model when evaluated on other datasets," as the authors describe.
The robustness advantage thus appears to be a property of training data diversity rather
than model scale specifically.

### 4.2 Comparison with Human Performance

To assess where Whisper sits relative to human transcribers, the authors computed a
*robustness frontier*: for each zero-shot Whisper model size, they plotted average WER on
three out-of-distribution datasets against WER on LibriSpeech. Supervised LibriSpeech
models cluster far above this frontier — they are less robust than expected given their
in-distribution performance. The estimated robustness frontier of zero-shot Whisper models
includes the 95% confidence interval for a single human evaluator's performance on those
same datasets.

A more direct comparison was conducted on 25 recordings from the Kincaid46 dataset,
a collection of diverse audio including scripted broadcast, unscripted interviews, telephone
calls, and meetings. Five professional transcription services provided reference transcripts:
four entirely human, one computer-assisted. The computer-assisted service achieved the
lowest aggregate WER, 1.15 percentage points lower than Whisper. The four purely human
transcription services performed only a fraction of a percentage point better than Whisper
on the same 25 recordings. The authors note that Whisper's English ASR performance is "not
perfect but very close to human-level accuracy."

### 4.3 Multilingual Speech Recognition

On Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS, Pratap et al., 2020b), which covers 8 European languages,
zero-shot Whisper achieves 7.3% WER, outperforming fine-tuned XLS-R (Babu et al., 2021)
at 10.9% and matching Maestro (Chen et al., 2022b) at 7.3%. On VoxPopuli (Wang et al.,
2021), covering 16 European languages, Whisper (13.6% WER) lags substantially behind
Maestro (8.1%), which the authors attribute to other models using VoxPopuli as a major
unsupervised pretraining source and to VoxPopuli having roughly 10× more supervised data
per language than MLS.

Performance across a broader language set was studied on the Fleurs dataset (Conneau et
al., 2022), covering 102 languages. A strong log-log linear relationship exists between
the amount of per-language training data and zero-shot WER (r² = 0.83), with WER
approximately halving for every 16-fold increase in training hours. Languages that deviate
from this trend — performing worse than predicted — tend to have unique scripts or are
linguistically distant from the Indo-European majority of the training set (Hebrew, Telugu,
Chinese, Korean). The training dataset is English-heavy due to internet data collection
biases, and most non-English languages have fewer than 1,000 hours of training data;
performance on low-resource languages remains correspondingly poor.

### 4.4 Speech-to-English Translation

On CoVoST 2 (Wang et al., 2020b), which covers translation from 21 source languages to
English, zero-shot Whisper achieves 29.1 BLEU overall, improving over mSLAM-CTC (24.8)
and Maestro (25.2). The advantage is most pronounced on low-resource languages: on the
lowest-resource group, Whisper achieves 25.2 BLEU versus mSLAM's 18.5, a gain of 6.7
BLEU attributable to the far larger translation training data in Whisper's pretraining set
(68,000 hours for these languages versus 861 total hours in CoVoST2's training split). On
high-resource languages, Whisper (36.2 BLEU) does not match Maestro (38.2) or mSLAM (37.8).
The authors caution that the text standardizer used in this evaluation was developed
alongside Whisper, which precludes confident state-of-the-art claims.

### 4.5 Language Identification

Zero-shot Whisper achieves 64.5% language identification accuracy on the Fleurs benchmark,
substantially below the supervised state of the art (mSLAM-CTC: 77.7%). However, this
comparison is confounded: Whisper has no training data for 20 of the 102 Fleurs languages,
placing a structural ceiling on its accuracy at 80.4%. On the 82 languages where Whisper
does have training data, it achieves 80.3% — within 0.1 percentage points of the ceiling.
Language identification performance is therefore primarily constrained by training data
coverage rather than representational capacity.

### 4.6 Long-form Transcription

Whisper's 30-second context window requires a sliding-window strategy for audio longer than
30 seconds: the window shifts according to the timestamps predicted by the model. The authors
developed decoding heuristics to reduce failure modes (repetition loops, hallucination):
5-beam search, temperature fallback when outputs are implausibly repetitive or have low
log-probability, voice activity detection to skip silent segments, and previous-text
conditioning for cross-window context continuity. Applied incrementally, these reduce average
WER across seven long-form datasets from 11.0% (greedy decoding only) to 10.0% (full
heuristic stack).

On those seven benchmarks — TED talks, podcasts, late-night television, earnings calls, and
recorded interviews — Whisper outperforms all compared open-source ASR models and performs
better than four commercial ASR services on most benchmarks. The authors note that some
commercial services may have been trained on portions of these publicly available datasets,
making the comparison approximate.

---

## 5. Analysis and Ablations

### 5.1 Model Scale

Performance improves with model size across multilingual speech recognition, translation,
and language identification for all five model sizes from 39 M to 1,550 M parameters. English
speech recognition shows diminishing returns at larger model sizes, consistent with the
hypothesis that English ASR is approaching a human-level performance ceiling where model
capacity is no longer the bottleneck.

### 5.2 Dataset Scale

A medium-sized model was trained on subsets ranging from 0.5% to 100% of the 680,000-hour
dataset to measure data scaling effects:

| Training Hours | English WER (↓) | Multilingual WER (↓) | X→En BLEU (↑) |
|---------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------|
| 3,405         | 30.5            | 92.4                | 0.2           |
| 6,811         | 19.6            | 72.7                | 1.7           |
| 13,621        | 14.4            | 56.6                | 7.9           |
| 27,243        | 12.3            | 45.0                | 13.9          |
| 54,486        | 10.9            | 36.4                | 19.2          |
| 681,070       | 9.9             | 29.2                | 24.8          |

*Table 2: All metrics improve monotonically with training data size. English WER is an
average over 12 evaluation datasets; multilingual WER covers overlapping Fleurs languages;
X→En BLEU is averaged over CoVoST2. (Source: Table 6 in Radford et al., 2022.)*

All three tasks improve monotonically across all data scales. Translation BLEU is near zero
at or below 7,000 hours — a minimum-data threshold for this task to become functional at all
— then follows a roughly log-linear trend. Multilingual WER follows a power-law improvement
through 54,000 hours. English WER improves rapidly from 3,000 to 13,000 hours then slows,
again consistent with approaching a saturation regime. At the largest scale (54,000 to
681,070 hours), all tasks show diminishing returns, which the authors interpret as either
under-training relative to dataset size or a genuine plateau in data-scaling benefits for
speech recognition.

### 5.3 Multitask and Multilingual Transfer

A natural concern with joint multitask training is *negative transfer*: interference between
tasks degrading performance on each individual task compared to a task-specific model. The
authors tested this by comparing English-only models with jointly trained models at equal
compute, adjusting for the fraction of compute devoted to English SR (65% in joint training).

At small model sizes, joint training does hurt English SR — negative transfer is real and
measurable. However, as model size and compute increase, joint models improve faster and
eventually surpass English-only models. At the largest experiments, joint training yields
slightly better English SR even without any compute adjustment. This pattern suggests that
exposure to diverse multilingual speech improves acoustic representations in ways that
benefit English SR, but only when the model is large enough to learn both without conflict.

### 5.4 Noise Robustness

Whisper was compared against 14 ASR models from the literature under additive white noise
and pub noise (ambient restaurant sound) across a range of signal-to-noise ratios (SNR).
Under low noise (40 dB SNR), many models outperform Whisper — expected, as those models
train primarily on clean LibriSpeech-style audio. Under high noise (SNR below 10 dB),
all 14 compared models perform worse than Whisper under pub noise. Whisper's robustness
advantage is thus most pronounced under the naturalistic distribution shifts that correspond
to real-world noisy environments.

### 5.5 Text Normalization Validity

The text normalizer used for WER computation was developed alongside Whisper, raising the
concern that it might discount formatting errors that Whisper specifically makes more often
than other models. Comparing against the independently developed FairSpeech normalizer
(Koenecke et al., 2020), the two normalizers produce similar relative WER differences on
most benchmarks. On three benchmarks — WSJ, CallHome, and Switchboard — the authors'
normalizer benefits Whisper noticeably more than it benefits comparison models, due to
specific formatting conventions (number expressions, common contractions) handled more
permissively. The authors acknowledge this evaluation bias on those specific benchmarks.

---

## 6. Discussion

### 6.1 Distributional Coverage as the Driver of Robustness

The central result — that a zero-shot model trained on diverse weakly labeled internet data
substantially outperforms a supervised model matched on an in-distribution benchmark —
points to a specific explanation for the ASR robustness gap: models trained on a single
dataset distribution learn dataset-specific patterns that generalize within that distribution
but not beyond it. This is a manifestation of "shortcut learning" (Geirhos et al., 2020):
the model solves the right task on the training distribution but learns the wrong
representation. Whisper's training distribution — 680,000 hours of internet audio spanning
thousands of environments, domains, languages, and recording conditions — acts as a
regularizer against any single such shortcut. The 55.2% average relative error reduction
over the supervised baseline measures how much benefit that distributional breadth provides
compared to in-distribution specialization.

### 6.2 Reframing the Comparison with Human Performance

A recurring claim in ASR research is that models have achieved "superhuman" performance on
LibriSpeech. The paper's authors argue that this comparison is misleading. The difference
between machine and human performance on a benchmark arises not from the test but from the
training: humans transcribing a benchmark audio sample have never been trained on
LibriSpeech-style audio, so they are tested for out-of-distribution generalization. A machine
model trained on LibriSpeech is tested for in-distribution generalization. Both are
evaluated on the same test data, but two different abilities are being measured.

This framing explains why zero-shot Whisper, not supervised LibriSpeech models, approaches
human robustness across benchmarks (Figure 2 in the paper): its training regime more closely
mirrors how humans develop speech competence — broad exposure to varied speech rather than
intensive practice on a specific narrow distribution.

### 6.3 Connection to Weak Supervision at Scale in Vision

Whisper's success is directly analogous to results from large-scale weak supervision in
computer vision. Models trained on internet images with noisy labels (Mahajan et al., 2018)
or on image-text pairs from the web (Radford et al., 2021; Kolesnikov et al., 2020) showed
dramatically improved robustness and zero-shot transfer. In both cases, the enabling factor
appears to be that internet-scale diversity forces the model to learn representations close
to the semantic content of the data, rather than dataset-specific surface features. Whisper
provides evidence that this principle extends from images to audio.

### 6.4 Limitations

**Fine-tuning not evaluated.** The entire study focuses on zero-shot transfer. For practical
deployments where labeled in-domain data is available, fine-tuning Whisper could improve
performance substantially beyond the zero-shot numbers reported here; this remains unstudied.

**Low-resource language performance.** The training dataset is English-heavy due to
internet data collection biases. Most non-English languages have fewer than 1,000 hours of
training data, and performance on low-resource languages remains poor. The strong scaling
law (r² = 0.83) makes clear that performance would improve with targeted data collection for
these languages, but this has not been done.

**Long-form decoding failures.** Hallucination, repetition loops, and failure to transcribe
the first or last few words of a segment are known failure modes of the sequence-to-sequence
generation approach used in long-form transcription. The heuristic decoding strategy
described in Section 4.6 substantially reduces these failures but does not eliminate them.

**Evaluation fairness.** The text normalizer was co-developed with Whisper, introducing
modest bias on some benchmarks (notably WSJ, CallHome, Switchboard). The comparison with
commercial ASR services is imperfect because those services may have trained on the
evaluation datasets. The human comparison uses only 25 recordings without reported confidence
intervals.

**Language identification.** While Whisper achieves 80.3% on languages it was trained on,
the overall Fleurs accuracy (64.5%) is substantially below the supervised state of the art
(77.7%), primarily because of the 20 languages for which Whisper has no training data.

---

## 7. Related Work

### 7.1 Scaling in Automatic Speech Recognition

Scale — of models, data, and compute — has consistently improved ASR performance over the
past decade. Deep Speech 2 (Amodei et al., 2015) scaled to 12,000 hours with distributed
GPU training. Narayanan et al. (2018) used semi-supervised pretraining to reach 162,000
hours of labeled audio. BigSSL (Zhang et al., 2021) pushed unsupervised pretraining to
1,000,000 hours with multi-billion-parameter fine-tuned models. Earlier weakly supervised
efforts (Chen et al., 2021; Galvez et al., 2021) scaled labeled speech to 10,000–30,000
hours. Whisper occupies a distinct point in this space: 680,000 hours of supervised
(though noisily labeled) pretraining without an unsupervised pretraining stage.

### 7.2 Self-supervised Speech Pretraining

wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020) demonstrated that self-supervised contrastive learning
on unlabeled audio could learn representations that, when fine-tuned with a supervised
decoder, compete with fully supervised baselines. HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021a) improved this
with masked prediction of pseudo-labels. XLS-R (Babu et al., 2021) scaled multilingual
self-supervised pretraining. These models share an important property that Whisper's
approach avoids: the pretrained encoder alone cannot produce transcripts; a separate
supervised decoder must be learned for each deployment distribution.

### 7.3 Multitask and Multilingual Learning for Speech

Multitask learning for speech has a long history. Toshniwal et al. (2018) jointly trained
a single model across multiple languages. Pratap et al. (2020a) scaled this to 50 languages
with a billion-parameter model. mSLAM (Bapna et al., 2022) extended joint pretraining to
cover both speech and text. Whisper's specific contribution is using a token-based
conditioning format to cover four heterogeneous speech processing tasks within a single
decoder without architectural changes, and demonstrating that at sufficient scale this
training is mutually beneficial across all tasks.

### 7.4 Robustness to Distribution Shift

The robustness of machine learning models to distribution shift has been studied across
image classification (Taori et al., 2020), natural language processing (Hendrycks et al.,
2020), and question answering (Miller et al., 2020). A consistent finding is that multi-domain
training improves robustness — a finding that Whisper confirms for speech at an
unprecedented scale. The connection to CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) is direct: both works
demonstrate that sufficiently large and diverse weakly supervised training can produce
zero-shot performance that matches task-specific supervised models on reference benchmarks
while far exceeding them on out-of-distribution evaluations.

---

## 8. Conclusion

Whisper demonstrates that the robustness gap between human and machine speech recognition
is not primarily a model capacity problem but a training distribution problem. A single
encoder-decoder Transformer trained on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised internet audio —
without self-supervised pretraining, without dataset-specific fine-tuning, and without data
augmentation — achieves 55.2% average relative error reduction over a comparable supervised
model on 13 diverse out-of-distribution benchmarks, approaches human accuracy on English
speech, reaches zero-shot performance competitive with or better than prior work on speech
translation and multilingual recognition, and outperforms commercial ASR systems on most
long-form transcription benchmarks.

The central lesson is that scaling weakly supervised pretraining with diverse internet data
has been underappreciated in speech recognition research relative to the dominant unsupervised
pretraining paradigm. Diverse supervised data at sufficient scale appears to produce the
same generalizable acoustic and linguistic representations that human listeners develop
through broad exposure to varied speech — and that breadth, not in-distribution
specialization, produces robust human-like performance.

Key open problems include improving performance on low-resource languages through targeted
data collection, addressing long-form transcription failure modes through better decoding
strategies, and studying the benefits of fine-tuning on specific deployment distributions.

---

# Audience Profile

**Mode:** B — Adjacent ML researcher

**Description:**
Machine-learning researchers from subfields other than speech processing (e.g., NLP,
computer vision, RL, reinforcement learning from human feedback). They understand general
deep learning concepts, Transformer architectures, standard supervised and self-supervised
training, sequence-to-sequence models, multitask learning, scaling behavior, distribution
shift, and zero-shot evaluation. They do NOT know: ASR-specific terminology (WER, CER,
hybrid ASR systems, language models in ASR), speech-specific benchmarks (LibriSpeech,
CommonVoice, CHiME, CORAAL, Fleurs, CoVoST2, VoxPopuli), prior ASR model families
(wav2vec, HuBERT, CTC, conformer), or the specific challenges of audio as an input modality.

**What they need explained:**
- Word error rate and its limitations as a metric
- Why evaluating ASR on a single dataset is misleading
- What "weakly supervised" means in the speech context specifically
- The LibriSpeech benchmark and its role as the community reference
- What a Mel spectrogram is (brief)
- Effective robustness as a framing concept
- Voice activity detection and language identification as tasks

**What they already know that we can use as analogies:**
- CLIP and image-text pretraining (analogous to Whisper's internet data approach)
- GPT-2/GPT-3 style language models (shared tokenizer)
- Multi-task learning and transfer learning in NLP
- Scaling laws from LLMs (data size vs. performance curves)
- Shortcut learning / spurious correlations in neural networks

**Binding personas:**
1. NLP researcher familiar with CLIP-style pretraining, curious about the speech equivalent
2. Computer vision researcher asking whether weak supervision at scale works as well for audio as for images

# Research Communication Objective

**Paper:** "Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision" (Radford et al., 2022)

**Deliverable:** Standalone research paper in Markdown for adjacent ML researchers (Mode B audience).

**Core claim to communicate:**
Training an encoder-decoder Transformer on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised internet
audio produces a speech recognition model that, evaluated zero-shot, achieves 55.2% average
relative error reduction over a supervised model matched on in-distribution performance —
across 13 diverse out-of-distribution benchmarks — and approaches human-level accuracy and
robustness on English speech.

**The one argument the reader must leave with:**
The robustness gap between human and machine speech recognition is a training distribution
problem, not a model capacity problem. Broad, diverse, weakly supervised data at scale
produces robustness that task-specific in-distribution training cannot.

**Why adjacent researchers should care:**
- Directly analogous to the CLIP result in vision: internet-scale weak supervision enables
  zero-shot generalization that matches specialized supervised baselines
- Reframes the meaning of "superhuman" benchmark performance (in-distribution ≠ generally capable)
- The scaling result is directly relevant to LLM-adjacent researchers thinking about
  data curation, training efficiency, and multitask generalization
- Released models serve as a strong multimodal backbone for further research

**What must NOT be overclaimed:**
- Fine-tuning performance is not studied; zero-shot results may be conservative
- Low-resource language performance is limited by training data, not the approach
- The human comparison uses a small sample (25 recordings) without confidence intervals
- Text normalizer co-development introduces modest evaluation bias on some benchmarks
- Language identification underperforms supervised SOTA due to missing training languages

**Success criterion:**
A reader who studies NLP or CV but not speech should finish the paper understanding:
(1) what the robustness problem in ASR is and why it matters,
(2) why existing approaches fail to solve it,
(3) how Whisper solves it and with what evidence,
(4) what the honest limitations are,
and should be able to describe the key result (55.2% RER) to a colleague.

- Text normalizer co-development introduces modest evaluation bias on some benchmarks
- Language identification underperforms supervised SOTA due to missing training languages

**Success criterion:**
A reader who studies NLP or CV but not speech should finish the paper understanding:
(1) what the robustness problem in ASR is and why it matters,
(2) why existing approaches fail to solve it,
(3) how Whisper solves it and with what evidence,
(4) what the honest limitations are,
and should be able to describe the key result (55.2% RER) to a colleague.
